structured_output.hypothesis: For blind or troglobitic cave species, the nearest relatives (congeners or confamilials) of North American cave species live on the surface or in caves of North America, and those of European cave species live in Europe, so cave faunas of the two continents are not specially similar to each other.
structured_output.pass_criterion: In a phylogeny or taxonomy-based test of at least 50 troglobitic species per continent, at least 80% of species on each continent have their closest genus-level or sister-group relative on the same continent. The share of cross-continental nearest-relative pairs between American and European cave species must also be below 10%, and significantly below the share expected under random assignment (Fisher exact test, p < 0.01).
structured_output.fail_criterion: Fewer than 60% of cave species on either continent have their nearest relative on the same continent. Alternatively, cave species of America and Europe pair with each other significantly more often than with their own continent's surface fauna (cross-continental pairing at or above 40%, Fisher exact p < 0.01).
structured_output.interpretation: Darwin's 'cave-animals' are troglobites: obligate subterranean species, usually blind and depigmented. His 'affinities' are taken as taxonomic or phylogenetic nearest relatives (the same genus or family, or a sister clade). 'America' is taken as North America, where the Mammoth Cave fauna he discussed lives, and 'Europe' as the European continent. The modern reinterpretation uses sister-group or genus membership rather than his 1859 judgement of similarity. Some cave taxa have Holarctic relatives, such as Cambarus and Astacus crayfish or Typhlichthys and Amblyopsis fishes. These must be coded as ambiguous and reported, not forced into either category.
structured_output.no_dataset_reason: I found no public dataset that holds troglobitic species from both North America and Europe together with their nearest-relative or phylogenetic placement, so I could not name one I had fetched. The nearest candidate I fetched was the Biodiversity Data Journal data paper 'Continental data on cave-dwelling spider communities across Europe (Arachnida: Araneae)' (https://bdj.pensoft.net/article/38492/). It covers Europe only, so it cannot test the America-versus-Europe comparison the claim needs, and I did not use it. The other regional sets I came across were the Tennessee troglobiont database, which is American only and has no dataset DOI, and the USGS Appalachian karst grids, which are American only. I did not fetch either. A GBIF occurrence search cannot isolate troglobites, because GBIF has no cave-obligate flag. Without a curated cave-species list, the claim cannot be tested from GBIF. Naming GBIF, or a single-continent dataset, would be a weakened version of the claim, so I am returning null.
